title: associate-ic-hiring-activation-and-skill-mapping
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working doc is a combined hiring plan + interview rubric + 30/60/90 onboarding checklist for Associate IC roles (Entry-level SWE / Junior ML infra) across Eng teams. Goal: reduce time-to-hire, standardize evaluation, and give a repeatable activation path so managers can ramp new hires to productive PRs within 90 days.

TL;DR summary:
- Hire for learning velocity + collaboration over deep domain experience.
- Two-stage screen (phone screen + pair-programming + take-home candidate optional) followed by a lightweight on-site loop (2 interviews + manager convo).
- Use a 5-point competency rubric but map to yes/no pass thresholds by role band.
- 30/60/90 checklist focused on access, readmes, small first-week wins, mentor checkpoints, and measurable ramp metrics.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Should we mandate a take-home exercise for all associates or make it optional by hiring manager? (Pros: signal, uniform; Cons: UX burden, bias)
- Leveling edge cases: how to handle strong CS grads w/o backend experience but good infra interest?
- Run this plan in pilot with Eng:console, Eng-serving-runtime, and Eng-observability first.

Hiring plan (timeline & owners):
- Requisition -> People ops posts draft JD (1–2 days)
- Sourcing window 2–4 weeks (should aim for 20–30 screened candidates)
- Initial phone screen by recruiter + 1 hiring manager/peer (30 mins)
- Pair-programming loop + culture fit + manager (2.5 hours total)
- Offer stage: comp calibrated by TA partner + hiring manager (3 business days target)
Owners: Recruiter (sourcing), Hiring Manager (tech loop design), People Ops (rubric & offer ops), Buddy (onboarding ops).

Interview structure and rubric (Associate IC):
Scoring: 1-5 per dimension (1 low, 5 high). Pass threshold: average >=3.5 AND no score <=2 on safety zones.
Dimensions:
- Problem solving & clarity (CS fundamentals): arrays/strings/basic graphs, complexity reasoning. Expect conceptual clarity, not algorithmic brilliance.
- Code correctness & style: readable, tests or assertions, explain choices.
- System/components intuition: basic client-server, REST, queues — ask small design Qs, expect tradeoffs.
- Collaboration & communication: gives/accepts feedback, explains thought process.
- Learning orientation & ownership: examples of quick learning, small project ownership, debugging mindset.
- Cultural fit (teamwork, inclusivity): short behavioral questions.

Sample questions & interviewer prompts:
Phone screen (recruiter+engineer, 30m):
- Tell me about a bug you tracked down — what steps did you take? (probe for root cause vs symptoms)
- Quick fizzbuzz-style coding live (5–8 min) or explain a simple algorithm.

Pair-programming (60m):
- Live problem: implement a simple cache LRU or dedupe-lines from stream. Focus: communication, incremental steps, tests.
- Follow-up: how would you make it durable? (open to ideas: write-ahead-log, persistence)

Systems sense interview (45m):
- Given a simple webhook ingestion pipeline that sometimes drops events, where would you look? (expect mention of retries, idempotency, visibility)

Behavioral/Manager (30m):
- Tell me about a time you received critical feedback. What did you change?
- What excites you about building infra?

Scoring knobs (hiring calibration):
- For Eng-serving-runtime we may weight system sense + ownership higher.
- For Eng-console we may weight collaboration + product intuition more.
- For very strong grads: accept weaker system answers if they demonstrate strong CS fundamentals + learning examples.

Take-home option (guidelines):
- Keep to 2–4 hours max. Focus on reading a short spec + implementing one small endpoint + tests. Provide a clear rubric for reviewers. Make it optional: explain to candidate upfront and give a pass/fail based primarily on completeness.

Offer & compensation notes:
- Use bands: Associate IC I / II. Associate I = new grads / <1 yr experience. II = 1–2 yrs with internship/full-time cycles.
- Approval: hiring manager + TA lead + People Ops approval.

Onboarding & 30/60/90 activation checklist (manager + buddy responsibilities):
Before day 1 (manager):
- Provision laptop image request, create email, Slack, GitHub, internal SSO.
- Create first-week PRD: "first-issue" curated list (readmes, small bug, test fix).
- Assign buddy (not direct manager) and schedule 1:1s through 90 days.
Day 0–7: first-week goals (owner: buddy + manager)
- Orientation: TL;DR product overview (30m) + infra tour (30m).
- Meet the team + quick intros to frequently used repos.
- Complete 2 small tasks: repo build success and a trivial PR (documentation, lint fix).
- Security & compliance training (complete by day 7).
- Shadowing: sit with buddy on code reviews for 2 sessions.

30-day goals (owner: manager):
- Complete first non-trivial ticket end-to-end (from issue to merged PR).
- Demonstrate ability to run CI locally & read basic telemetry dashboards.
- Present a 10-minute "walkthrough" of the code changes they made.
- Manager 30-day check: OKR-lite alignment & skill gaps identified.

60-day goals:
- Independently own a small component or feature and ship it with minimal bugs.
- Submit at least 5 PRs with peer-reviewed feedback implemented.
- Start contributing to on-call rotations or runbook updates (shadow first).

90-day goals:
- Deliver a measurable improvement (perf, flakiness, docs) with before/after metrics.
- Manager determines full clearance to move to "independent contributor" expectations.
- Career conversation: next steps, growth plan, mentorship aim.

Ramp metrics (quantitative where possible):
- Time to first merged PR: target <= 14 days.
- Time to first independent feature: target <= 60 days.
- Peer review turn-around time for their PRs: average <= 48 hours.
- Mentor 1:1 frequency: weekly first month, biweekly thereafter.

First-90 Checklist (practical items):
- Accounts & access: SSO, GitHub org, CI tokens, monitoring dashboard read access, Slack channels (#eng-oncall, #eng-new-hires).
- Documentation: product-readme, repo contributing.md, architecture-exec-summary.
- Tools: local dev environment guide, test harness commands, docker/devcontainer instructions.
- Training: security, data handling, code review standards, ship checklist.
- Meetups: 30-min Friday demo slot at week 4; 1:1s scheduled.

Mentorship structure & expectations:
- Buddy: day-to-day help, code review buddy for first 4 weeks.
- Mentor (senior IC): career growth conversations, monthly check-ins, guide on impact projects.
- Manager: career goal setting + performance feedback.

Manager playbook snippets (shortcuts):
- Assign a "first-repo" with clear starter issues pre-labeled.
- Use pairing sessions for the first two feature tickets to model expectations.
- Keep first performance conversation informal and supportive — focus on strengths & 1-2 concrete growth items.

Inclusive hiring notes (non-negotiables):
- Panel diversity where possible; use structured interviews and avoid hypothetical-only questions.
- Clear rubric shared among interviewers before loop begins.
- Reasonable accommodations: explicitly offer code editor choices, extra time if needed for take-home.

Admin templates (copy/paste for use):
- Recruiter email template: "Hi {name}, we're excited about your application for Associate IC at Redwood Inference. Next step: 30m screening with our engineer. Please share availability…"
- Interviewer prompt: "You have 60 minutes. Start by outlining approach for 3–5 minutes, then code incrementally, vocalize tradeoffs. Focus on correctness and clarity; it's okay to ask clarifying Qs."
- Manager 30/60/90 email to new hire: short checklist + links to resources + first 1:1 schedule.

Pilot metrics & follow-up plan:
- Pilot with 6 hires across 3 eng subteams; track time-to-offer, offer acceptance rate, time-to-first-PR, new-hire NPS at day 30.
- Retro at week 8 with hiring managers, recruiters, and mentors.

Appendix: quick rubric cheat-sheet (for interviewers)
- Problem solving: 5 = breaks into subproblems, explains complexity, finds optimal approach; 3 = workable but some inefficiencies; 1 = no clear approach.
- Code/style: 5 = clean, tests or edge-case handling; 3 = passes basic cases; 1 = messy/unreadable.
- Collaboration: 5 = invites feedback, adapts; 3 = OK; 1 = dismissive.

Last notes: keep this doc short, iterate based on pilot. Will convert successful bits into templated checklists in Notion and reproducible onboarding repo scripts.

-- Priya (people ops) — draft for feedback from: Evan, Lina, Maya.
